pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Series vs parallel circuits

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** KS3 'Current electricity' — statutory wording 'electric current... in circuits, series and parallel circuits, currents add where branches meet and current as flow of charge' and 'potential difference, measured in volts, battery and bulb ratings' (verified by fetch); the series/parallel contrast and the 'currents add where branches meet' rule are explicitly KS3. NOTE the KS2→KS3 progression: KS2 Year 6 is SERIES only, and parallel is first met here.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** no middle-school PE covers series/parallel DC-circuit analysis, so this is UK-ANCHORED (state honestly).

- **Operational details:** At KS2 the child built SERIES circuits only; this topic introduces the PARALLEL configuration and the contrasting rules for current and voltage in each, plus why the choice matters in practice (household wiring). The rules to secure: in SERIES the current is the same everywhere and the voltages across components ADD UP to the supply; in PARALLEL each branch gets the FULL supply voltage and the branch currents ADD where they meet. The deepest, most counter-intuitive idea — worth foregrounding — is that adding a parallel branch LOWERS the total resistance and RAISES the total current (more routes for charge), the opposite of adding components in series. Teaching is most effective as a structured contrast: build the same components two ways, place meters at several points, predict-then-test, and tie each rule to a practical consequence (parallel keeps every device at full brightness and independently switchable; one failing does not kill the rest).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal-operational / quantitative, ~12–13).
bestPractices: Teach by structured CONTRAST, not two separate topics: build the same two bulbs in series and in parallel side by side, so each rule is learned against its opposite.

Tie every rule to a meter reading at several points: SERIES — ammeters everywhere read the same, voltmeters across components add to the supply; PARALLEL — voltmeters across each branch read the full supply, ammeters in the branches add to the main current (the KS3 'currents add where branches meet').

Foreground the counter-intuitive resistance result: adding a parallel branch gives charge MORE routes, so total resistance DROPS and total current RISES — directly opposite to adding a series component. Predict before testing to surface the wrong intuition.

Anchor 'why parallel for homes' in observable consequences: each device gets the full mains voltage (so full brightness/power), each can be switched independently, and one failing leaves the others working — contrast old series fairy-lights (one blows, all go out) with parallel wiring.

Use predict-then-test relentlessly: 'add a second bulb in series — what happens to the brightness of the first?' (both dim, current drops); 'add a second bulb in parallel — what happens to the first?' (unchanged, still full brightness; total current rises).

Keep the rules causal, not just memorised: series bulbs share the supply voltage (so each gets less → dimmer); parallel bulbs each get the whole supply (so each stays bright), and the cell delivers more total current.

Guard against the resurfacing current-used-up error in series — in a series loop the current is reduced but still the SAME at every point; the bulbs are equally bright, not brighter nearest the battery.
keyRepresentations: Side-by-side series vs parallel diagrams of the SAME components, with ammeters and voltmeters placed at multiple points and their readings shown.
A junction close-up where branch currents ADD where they meet (the KS3 phrase made visual).
Brightness comparison — two bulbs in series (both dimmer than one) vs two in parallel (each as bright as one), with the supply voltage shared vs full.
Household/parallel wiring schematic — appliances each across the full supply, independently switched, with the 'unscrew one, the rest stay on' consequence.
A total-resistance dial — adding series components pushes resistance up and current down; adding parallel branches pulls total resistance down and current up.
commonMisconceptions: Mixing up which quantity is shared vs added — e.g. thinking voltage is the same everywhere in series, or that current splits but voltage adds in parallel; the rules are crossed between the two configurations.
Believing current splits EQUALLY at a parallel junction regardless of the branches — it divides according to resistance, with more current through the lower-resistance branch.
Thinking adding a parallel branch reduces the total current — it INCREASES it (lower total resistance, more routes for charge).
Expecting parallel bulbs to be dimmer than a single bulb — each branch gets the full supply voltage, so each is as bright as a lone bulb (unlike series, where they share and dim).
The current-used-up error resurfacing in series — thinking the bulb nearest the battery is brighter; in series the current is the same everywhere and identical bulbs are equally bright.
Assuming more components always means more total resistance — true in series, FALSE in parallel, where adding branches LOWERS the total resistance.
Thinking household circuits are series — they are parallel, so each appliance gets full voltage and works independently.

learn.summary: Teach series vs parallel circuits (ages 12–13) by structured CONTRAST of the SAME two bulbs built both ways, tying each rule to meter readings at several points and to a practical consequence. Secure: in series the current is the same everywhere and component voltages add to the supply; in parallel each branch gets the full supply voltage and branch currents add where they meet. Foreground the counter-intuitive result that adding a parallel branch LOWERS total resistance and RAISES total current — the opposite of adding a series component. Use predict-then-test relentlessly (add/remove a bulb, watch brightness and meters) and anchor 'why homes are wired in parallel' in observable consequences. A recomputing circuit simulation (or a hands-on physical build) is the central activity; a comparison quiz, an annotated diagram-pair reference, and an electrician design dialogue are complementary. This is a UK KS3-anchored topic (parallel first met here after KS2 series-only); no middle-school NGSS PE covers series/parallel DC-circuit analysis.

activities.title: Build it both ways: series and parallel on the same two bulbs
feedback: If a learner predicts the series bulb nearest the battery is brighter: place ammeters before and after it — the readings agree, so current is not 'used up'; identical bulbs carry the same current and share the supply voltage equally, so they are equally dim.

If a learner predicts a parallel bulb dims when you add another branch: each branch gets the FULL supply voltage, so the first is unchanged; it is the current that adds, not the voltage that splits (for an ideal cell).
If a learner predicts both parallel bulbs go out when one is removed: trace each branch — every parallel branch is its own complete loop to the cell, so breaking one leaves the other intact.

If a learner expects adding a parallel branch to reduce total current: more routes mean lower total resistance and therefore MORE total current; contrast with series where adding a component raises resistance and lowers current.
activities.rationale: Series-vs-parallel is a comparison of live behaviours — brightness, meter readings, and add/remove consequences — that a recomputing simulation can display and the learner can probe. Building both from the same components and predicting before testing surfaces and overturns the crossed-rules and resistance misconceptions. A live-recomputing model and multi-point meters are the mechanism that makes each rule visible; a static diagram can state the rules but not show the readings or consequences change. Hands-on physical circuits with real bulbs, cells and meters achieve the same contrast.
sourceClaims: Crossed series/parallel rules, the belief that adding a parallel branch reduces current, expecting parallel bulbs to be dimmer, and the resurfacing current-used-up error are documented difficulties best tackled by structured contrast, multi-point meter readings, and predict-then-test with add/remove consequences.
learnerActions: Start with one bulb lit from a cell; note its brightness as a baseline.
Add a SECOND bulb IN SERIES; before testing, predict what happens to the first bulb's brightness, then observe (both dim together) and watch the ammeter reading fall.
Reconfigure the same two bulbs into PARALLEL; predict first, then observe the first bulb stays at full brightness (ideal cell) while the main-line current rises.
Place an ammeter at several points: in series confirm all readings are equal; in parallel confirm the branch currents add to the main-line current where branches meet.
Place a voltmeter across components: in series confirm the component voltages add to the supply; in parallel confirm each branch reads the full supply voltage.
Do the unscrew/remove test: remove one bulb in series (whole circuit goes dark) and in parallel (the other stays lit); trace the loop for the remaining parallel bulb to see it is still complete.
If a total-resistance readout is available, compare it as you add a series component (resistance up, current down) vs a parallel branch (resistance down, current up).
Try a household mode wiring appliances across the full supply in parallel, switching each independently.
activities.intendedInsight: Series and parallel obey crossed rules: series shares the voltage (bulbs dimmer, current same everywhere, one break kills all) while parallel gives each branch the full voltage on its own loop (full brightness with an ideal cell, currents add, independent switching). Adding a parallel branch opens more routes for charge, so total resistance drops and total current rises. Houses are wired in parallel because each device gets the full supply voltage and can be switched, or can fail, independently.

activities.title: Sort and predict: series vs parallel rules
feedback: For a mis-sort crossing the rules: re-pair each quantity with its configuration — in series the current is the same everywhere and the supply voltage is shared, so component voltages add to the supply; in parallel each branch gets the full supply voltage and branch currents add where they meet.
For 'adding a parallel branch reduces total current': it increases it, because total resistance drops with more routes.
For 'parallel bulbs are dimmer': each branch sees the full supply, so each is as bright as a lone bulb (ideal cell).
activities.rationale: Stating what is shared vs added, predicting brightness, and choosing a configuration for a purpose are well-defined checks that target the crossed-rules and resistance misconceptions. The sort can check whether rules are stated and matched, but it does not by itself elicit reasoning through live brightness and meter changes, so it is best used after hands-on or simulated building.
sourceClaims: Crossed series/parallel rules, the belief that adding a parallel branch reduces current, expecting parallel bulbs to be dimmer, and the resurfacing current-used-up error are documented difficulties best tackled by structured contrast, multi-point meter readings, and predict-then-test with add/remove consequences.
learnerActions: Sort statements into SERIES vs PARALLEL columns: 'current same everywhere', 'voltages across components add to the supply', 'each branch gets the full supply voltage', 'branch currents add where they meet'.
Predict the brightness of the first bulb when a second bulb is added in series, then when added in parallel.
Answer 'why is household wiring parallel?' and justify by a consequence (full voltage to each device, independent switching, one failing leaves others working).
Predict what happens to the total current when a parallel branch is added.
Rank circuits by total resistance as series components are added vs as parallel branches are added.
activities.intendedInsight: The rules and their practical consequences can be stated precisely and matched to the correct configuration, consolidating the contrast learned by building.

activities.title: Reference diagram pair: the rules at a glance
feedback: If a learner reads the parallel diagram as 'voltage splits': re-read the branch voltmeter labels — each branch shows the full supply.

If a learner thinks series bulbs differ in brightness because of their position: the equal ammeter readings along the loop show the current is the same everywhere, so identical bulbs are equally bright.
activities.rationale: A static annotated pair can present the rules and the household case as a reference summary. It states rather than demonstrates: it cannot show brightness changing or meters updating, so it works best beside the simulation or physical build, not instead of it.
learnerActions: Study a labelled pair of diagrams of the SAME components in series and in parallel, with meters placed at multiple points.
On the series diagram, note 'current same everywhere / component voltages add to supply'; on the parallel diagram, note 'each branch full supply voltage / branch currents add at the junction'.
Reveal the 'unscrew one' outcome for each: series goes dark, parallel keeps the rest lit.
Use the junction close-up to see branch currents adding where they meet.
activities.intendedInsight: A compact reference ties the crossed rules and the household-wiring case to clear diagrams, supporting recall after the active work.

activities.title: Electrician's design problem: series or parallel?
feedback: If a learner picks series for the house 'to save wire': point to the consequence — shared voltage means dimmer devices and one failure breaks the whole loop.
If a learner cannot justify parallel: prompt them to trace what happens to each other device when one branch is removed.
activities.rationale: A Socratic design dialogue can probe the practical choice and the misconceptions and press for consequence-based reasoning. The underlying rules are felt most strongly through manipulation and meter readings, so this works best as a debrief around the building activity rather than the sole route to the rules.
learnerActions: Take on real design problems with an electrician persona: how to wire old-style fairy lights vs a house lighting circuit.

Argue, for each case, whether series or parallel is appropriate and give the consequence-based reason (does one failing kill the rest? does each device get full voltage? can each be switched independently?).
Explain why a house is NOT wired in series by describing what would go wrong if one lamp failed.
Contrast old series fairy-lights (one blows, all go out) with parallel wiring.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing a configuration for a real purpose forces the learner to reason from the rules to consequences, reinforcing why parallel is standard for independent, full-brightness, fault-tolerant devices.

constraints: UK KS3-anchored: parallel is first met here after KS2 Year 6 series-only work; no middle-school NGSS performance expectation covers series/parallel DC-circuit analysis — state this honestly.

Keep brightness/full-voltage claims in the context of an ideal (negligible internal resistance) cell; with a real cell, adding parallel branches draws more current and can slightly reduce terminal voltage. Treat 'each parallel bulb stays at full brightness' as the ideal-cell idealisation, not a universal law.
Current divides between parallel branches according to resistance, NOT equally regardless of the branches — more current flows through the lower-resistance branch.
Guard against the current-used-up error: in a series loop the current is reduced overall but the SAME at every point, so identical bulbs are equally bright, not brighter near the battery.
The recognition/sorting quiz checks whether rules can be stated and matched; it does not by itself show the learner can reason through live brightness and meter changes — pair it with building.

The reference diagram pair and the dialogue state or discuss the rules; they do not let the learner observe readings and consequences change, so they are scaffolds/consolidation, not substitutes for building a working or simulated circuit.

Live-recomputing simulation, drag-in meters, live recolouring of brightness, a total-resistance readout and a household mode are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — offer them where available, but do not treat any one interaction as mandatory. Hands-on physical circuits with real bulbs, cells, ammeters and voltmeters achieve the same contrast.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source IOP claim (crossed rules, parallel-reduces-current belief, dimmer-parallel belief, current-used-up error) is marked verified:false in the row; the two DfE/NGSS curriculum claims are marked verified:true. Evidence strength is carried over unchanged, not upgraded.

The row repeatedly asserts parallel bulbs stay at 'full brightness'; this holds for an ideal cell. With a real cell, internal resistance means more total current can lower terminal voltage slightly. The activities keep the ideal-cell idealisation and this caveat is flagged in constraints; do not teach 'always exactly full brightness' as a universal law.

The original artefact-fit entries for a static image, dialogue and 3D included strong comparative/necessity phrasing ('only a recomputing sim can show', '3D adds nothing', 'weakly conveyed by talk'). These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordances and limits.

The KS3 curriculum claim was kept out of the per-activity sourceClaims of the building and electrician activities because it supports only the topic/content status, not those activities' medium/pedagogical rationales; the curriculum anchoring is preserved in the summary and constraints.

The IOP claim is retained on the sort/predict activity only because that activity includes predict-then-test of add/remove consequences named in the claim; it must not be read as evidence that the sort alone is sufficient to overturn the misconceptions.

The 'total-resistance DOWN, current UP when adding a parallel branch' result is physically correct for added resistive branches across a fixed supply and is retained as an outcome to predict-then-test, not merely asserted.
The 3D-interactive option was dropped from activities as redundant (a 2D schematic or physical build already conveys the topology); this is a catalog-ranking omission, not a pedagogical law.

assess.poeTask: With two identical bulbs in a parallel circuit, both lit, ask the child to predict what happens to the SECOND bulb when you unscrew the first, AND why. The 'all connected, so all go off' child predicts it goes dark; the independent-loops child predicts it stays lit. Then unscrew one to reveal.
probeDeeper: Put an ammeter before and after the first bulb in the series circuit. What will the two readings be, and what does that prove about 'using up' current?
Why does your house use parallel wiring rather than series — what would go wrong with series if one light failed?
Counterexample: in the parallel circuit you unscrew one bulb. Trace the loop for the OTHER bulb — is it still complete?
In series the voltages across the two bulbs add up to the battery voltage; in parallel each bulb has the full battery voltage. How does that explain the brightness difference?
assess.correctAnswer: In series the two bulbs share the battery's voltage, so each is dimmer than a single bulb; and because it's one loop, unscrewing either one breaks the loop and BOTH go out. In parallel each bulb gets the full battery voltage across its own branch, so each is as bright as a single bulb and the branches are independent — unscrew one and the other stays lit. That full voltage and independence is why household wiring is parallel.

errorPatterns.pattern: In series the first bulb is brighter because it gets the current first and 'uses some up' before the second ('the electricity runs down along the loop').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Current is the same everywhere in a series loop (ammeters agree); the bulbs are equally dim because they SHARE the voltage, not because current is consumed.
errorPatterns.distractor: The bulb nearer the battery is brighter because it gets the current first and uses some up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts unequal brightness in series, with the nearer bulb brighter.

errorPatterns.pattern: Unscrewing one bulb in parallel makes the other go out too, because they're on the same battery ('they're all connected, so all go off').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Each parallel branch is its own complete loop to the cell; breaking one leaves the other loop intact — trace both loops.
errorPatterns.distractor: If you unscrew one parallel bulb, the other goes out too, because they share the battery.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts both parallel bulbs die when one is removed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adding bulbs in parallel splits the voltage so each parallel bulb is dimmer, just like series ('more bulbs, less each, always').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Parallel branches each get the FULL supply voltage; it's the current that adds, not the voltage that splits — each bulb is at full brightness (ideal cell).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts parallel bulbs are dimmer than a single bulb.

responseLevels.gap: Uses a current-consumption or equal-sharing story — predicts unequal series brightness, or that removing one parallel bulb kills the other.
responseLevels.full: Explains series bulbs share voltage (equally dim, both die if one breaks) and parallel bulbs each get full voltage on independent loops (full brightness, independent), and connects this to why homes use parallel wiring.
responseLevels.partial: States the series/parallel rules and knows household wiring is parallel, but can't apply them to the brightness comparison or the unscrew-one case, or reverts to 'current used up'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You have two identical bulbs. In circuit A they're in series; in circuit B they're in parallel, both on the same battery. Compare how bright the bulbs are in A versus B, and explain what happens to EACH bulb if you unscrew one of the two.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks current is 'used up' or 'shared equally regardless' predicts unequal series brightness or that removing one parallel bulb changes the other; the rules-based child predicts equally-dim series bulbs (both die together) and full-brightness independent parallel bulbs. The reason tier separates a consumption/sharing story from a voltage-distribution story.
